# Preface: How to Use This Book {.unnumbered epub:type=preface}



Change one number in a dataset, and how many documents are now wrong? If the number was
copied by hand into a report, a slide, an email and a web page, nobody knows without
searching. This book teaches a way of publishing with nothing to search for: you write once,
in plain text, and a web page, a Word document, a PDF, slides, an e-book, a website, a blog
and a dashboard all rebuild from that one source with one command. The program that rebuilds
them is Quarto.

## Prompt, Check, Publish {.unnumbered #prompt-check-publish}

The title names the method, a loop you run at every step of every project. You **prompt** a
*coding agent*, a program that writes files and runs commands at your request, describing
one small piece of work with its files and columns named. It is an *agent*, not a chat,
because it acts: where a web chat replies with code for you to copy and run, an agent edits
your files and runs the commands itself, then reports back. You **check** what it did: read
what changed, look at the result, compare it with the data. An agent can be fluent, fast
and wrong, so this step is never skipped, and it is always yours. Then Quarto **publishes**,
rebuilding every output from the checked source the same way every time. @sec-quarto explains
why the last step can be trusted, and @sec-assistant how to make the first two reliable.

Every hands-on step that prompts an agent goes once round the loop in @fig-loop.

![Prompt, Check, Publish: the loop this book teaches, with who acts at each step.](media/diagrams/loop){#fig-loop .on-light fig-alt="The loop. Prompt: you ask a coding agent for one small step, naming the files and ending with a check; Chapter 2. The agent does the work: it writes files and runs commands. Check: you read what changed, open the result and compare it with the data; Chapter 2. If it is not right, you fix the prompt and go round again. The checked source goes to Publish: Quarto's quarto render rebuilds every output, the same way every time; Chapter 1. Then the next step begins with a new prompt. Small steps, each one checked, every output rebuilt from one source."}

Two more tools complete the method: Git records every version of the source, and a host such
as GitHub Pages puts the result on the web. The agent does the typing for all three.

## Find your path {.unnumbered #reading-paths}

You need not read the book in order. Find your role in the cards below and read the chapters
it lists; each path ends at a finished output and skips what was written for someone else.
Every path starts with @sec-quarto and @sec-assistant, which are short and are the method.

::: cards
New to the terminal

:   Read: @sec-setup, @sec-first-report, Part II (@sec-markdown to @sec-publish), then the water
    analysis (@sec-water-question onwards).\
    You finish with: the London guide on its own website.

A student

:   Read: @sec-ai-policy, @sec-setup, @sec-first-report, Part II, then the afterword's
    [coursework report](afterword.qmd#sec-project-coursework).\
    You finish with: a coursework report a marker can rebuild.

An educator

:   Read: @sec-setup, @sec-first-report, Part II (@sec-markdown to @sec-publish), and then
    the workshop in @sec-workshop.\
    You finish with: the London guide as a website, and the workshop to teach it.

An analyst who produces recurring reports

:   Read: @sec-fast-path and @sec-results, with the afterword's
    [metrics brief](afterword.qmd#sec-project-metrics) as where you are heading; if the
    terminal or Git is new to you, @sec-setup and @sec-first-report first.\
    You finish with: a brief in HTML and Word that rebuilds from next month's data.

A researcher or graduate student

:   Read: @sec-ai-policy, @sec-fast-path (after @sec-setup and @sec-first-report if the terminal
    is new), @sec-results, then the water analysis (@sec-water-question onwards).\
    You finish with: an analysis published as a report, slides and a website, and a
    [research supplement](afterword.qmd#sec-project-supplement).

A data scientist, or an ML, AI or research engineer

:   Read: @sec-fast-path, then @sec-results.\
    You finish with: an evaluation report and a model card from one results file, on a branch
    ready for review.

A software engineer

:   Read: @sec-fast-path, the checks of @sec-results-checks, CI in @sec-team, then the
    afterword's [design document](afterword.qmd#sec-project-rfc).\
    You finish with: a report added to a repository on a branch, with a guard, and a check that
    rebuilds it on every pull request.

A technical founder, or an early team

:   Read: @sec-fast-path, @sec-results, @sec-parameters and @sec-at-work, then the afterword's
    [investor update](afterword.qmd#sec-project-investor).\
    You finish with: an evaluation report and model card that investors and customers can
    check, and a monthly investor update that renders itself.

:::

Part I fits in an afternoon, and it ends with something to show for it. @sec-quarto and
@sec-assistant are reading, with nothing to install or type. If a terminal and Git are routine
and the fast path's tools are installed, @sec-fast-path takes you from there to a report in
three formats in under an hour. Otherwise @sec-setup sets up your computer in six steps, each
with a check you can see, in about an hour, and in @sec-first-report, about 45 minutes at the
keyboard, you render a real report by hand and find its one wrong number. If a step goes wrong
on the way, that is expected, and the book is built for it
([When you get stuck](#when-you-fall-behind)).

**The core path.** Parts II and V are long because they explain, but their core is shorter.
Read Part II from @sec-markdown to @sec-publish, and Part V, copying each block's finished
script from clustering on (@sec-routes); from Part III, @sec-results is enough. Leave for
later the sections marked *(optional)* in their headings and the water analysis's further
challenges: nothing later depends on them.

The book grew out of a six-hour workshop and keeps its shape; @sec-workshop has the day's
agenda and the chapters each block covers.

## Who this book is for {.unnumbered}

I wrote this book for analysts, researchers, data scientists, machine-learning engineers,
technical founders, educators and students: anyone who works with data and code and needs to
share the results. Most of all it is for people who publish numbers that change: the analyst
whose monthly pack is copied into Word and PowerPoint by hand, the researcher whose figures must
survive a resubmission, the engineer who writes up every evaluation three times, for a report,
a deck and a page, and the founder who sends investors a figure from the wrong month. It shows
how to publish everything from one plain-text source, prose and code together, with Quarto.
Quarto is free and open source, and it is traditional software, not AI, so the same source
builds the same report, slide deck or web page every time, as long as its packages are pinned,
its random seeds fixed and its data unchanged (@sec-reproducible): reproducible, interactive
and of publication quality. Along the way, I explain the concepts, the arguments and the
decisions behind each step.

Reproducibility is why I wrote this book: work that others can rebuild earns their trust and
gives them something to build on. Publishing is half the job; the other half is being read, so
the book treats every output as something a particular reader will use, and checks it as that
reader would. For a start-up, the method pays where the numbers change: the monthly investor
update, the evaluation white paper, the per-customer report, the documentation site. It pays
less where design or co-editing dominates: the designed pitch deck, the marketing site and the
plan the co-founders comment on in a shared document can stay where they are
(@sec-wrong-tool; the full case is @sec-at-work-startup).

You may be new to Quarto, to coding agents or to both. No programming is assumed: I explain
the Python the agent writes, but you do not have to write it. If the terminal is new to you,
@sec-setup teaches the little you need, one checked step at a time, and @sec-first-report has
you use it by hand on a real report before you give an agent its first edit. @sec-terminal
collects the keys, paths and error messages worth knowing. The book's code is Python; Quarto
runs R just as well, through knitr, but this book does not teach it.

You will need a computer on which you can install software (Windows, Mac or Linux), a free
GitHub account, and an account with one coding agent (@sec-facts lists what each accepts). If
you cannot install software, a ready-made environment in your browser will do
(@sec-codespace), and @sec-before-setup gives a route to an agent that costs nothing.

## The three running examples {.unnumbered}

Every concept is tied to one of three projects, each built on real, cited data.

::: cards
A London visitor guide (Part II)

:   For the city's tourism office, you write one guide that becomes a web page, a Word brief
    for partners, a printed flyer, a dashboard for managers and a published website. Every
    visitor number in it, from the 7\,116\,929 visits to the Natural History Museum \(South Kensington\) in
    2025 down, is computed from the counts published by the Association of
    Leading Visitor Attractions.

A model evaluation at a start-up (the fast path and Part III)

:   Acme Signals, a fictional two-person company, ranks a bank's marketing contacts for its call
    centre and evaluates each release of its model on the real UCI Bank Marketing data. You add
    Quarto to its existing repository and publish one set of results as an evaluation report
    and a model card, every number read from the results its own script computes.

Drinking-water risk in Colombian municipalities (the water analysis, Part V)

:   You group Colombia's municipal zones into kinds by water safety, services and context, from
    2016 to 2023, compare health and education outcomes
    between the kinds, and publish the analysis as a report, slides, a blog post and a website,
    all from one analysis script. Most of the data are Colombian open data, joined by official
    municipality codes; rainfall comes from the Climate Hazards Center's CHIRPS data and
    altitude from NASA's SRTM elevation data (@sec-sources).

:::

## How the book is organised {.unnumbered}

- **Part I** covers what you need first: what Quarto does (@sec-quarto) and how to work with a
  coding agent safely (@sec-assistant), then one of two routes. The fast path (@sec-fast-path)
  adds Quarto to an existing repository; the route from zero sets up your computer (@sec-setup)
  and has you check, record and undo a first report by hand (@sec-first-report).
- **Part II** builds the London guide, one format at a time: the foundations in depth.
- **Part III** is the craft of the outputs professionals are asked for, from one set of
  evaluation results.
- **Part IV** takes them into a team and an organisation: pull requests, continuous
  integration, confidential data and approved tools.
- **Part V**, the water analysis, builds a full analysis with the statistics explained on the
  way, following one municipality, Tunja, from raw rows to a council's last slide.

Each project ends by changing an input or a setting and explaining what the rebuild changed.
The **afterword** offers five projects that carry the method into your own work, a metrics
brief, a research supplement, a coursework report, a monthly investor update and a design
document with live numbers, each rebuilt from a fresh copy of its repository
([Afterword](afterword.qmd#sec-afterword)). The appendices hold the Windows setup, the
terminal's keys and habits, a cheatsheet, troubleshooting, every checkpoint, the data sources,
how this book is built, and the facts that change, with their dates.

By the end of the book you will be able to:

- explain how Quarto turns one source into many formats, and what it takes for every rebuild
  to give the same result;
- direct a coding agent safely: a folder of its own, written rules, one step per prompt, each
  ending in a check, and larger tasks only when their checks can run without you;
- add Quarto to an existing repository, and review an agent's change as a pull request and a
  fresh clone;
- publish one set of results to several readers, guarding every sentence whose words depend
  on the data;
- predict which outputs a changed input will update, and check that the rebuild did exactly
  that.

## What a hands-on step looks like {.unnumbered #how-the-hands-on-parts-work}

Each step is a three-part box, explained in @sec-boxes: the exact prompt to give your
agent, what it will probably run, and the few things only you can do. Prompts are
examples, not transcripts: agents vary, so check the result rather than the wording. Five
kinds of aside step out of the main text; here is one of each.

::: why
A number computed from the data cannot drift from them: every render computes it again.
Asides like this one explain the mechanism behind a step, so that you can adapt it to your own
project.
:::

::: pitfall
A render started while a live preview is rendering the same file collides with it. Asides
like this one describe failures seen in practice, and how to avoid them.
:::

::: practice
Ask for one step per prompt: a small change is quick to check, and when something breaks you
know which step broke it. Asides like this one hold judgement calls and habits.
:::

::: think
The agent reports a render with no errors. Is the work checked?

Not yet: a clean render proves that the code ran, not that its numbers are right. Asides like
this one ask a question to answer before you read on; the answer follows it.
:::

::: tryit
Asides like this one are exercises. Think of one document you produce more than once, and
note where each of its numbers comes from.

::: done
you can say which of its numbers are typed by hand and which come from a file.
:::
:::

Three more boxes appear in the chapters: a story from the build log, a true incident from the
making of this book; an illustration, a composite scene labelled as one; and "What you will
build", a picture of a chapter's finished output. Steps marked *optional* are for readers who
are ahead; nothing later depends on them.

## When you get stuck {.unnumbered #when-you-fall-behind}

You will get stuck: an install fails, a prompt goes wrong, a render stops with an error you
have never seen. Every hands-on block ends at a *checkpoint*, a folder of the workshop's files
(`checkpoints/`, downloaded in @sec-step-check) that holds the project as it should be at that
point, with a README listing the steps to catch up. The rule
is simple: **stuck for two minutes, catch up**. Where the book reaches a checkpoint, a catch-up
box gives the one line to paste into your agent (@fig-catch-up).

Reading on your own, spend a few minutes on a diagnosis first. Each step uses only what
@sec-setup and @sec-first-report teach:

1. **Where are you?** `pwd` prints the folder; the project's commands work only inside it.
2. **What changed?** `git status` lists the files changed since your last commit, and
   `git diff` shows how, including changes you did not mean to make.
3. **What does the error say?** Read its first line
   ([Reading an error](appendices/b-terminal.qmd#sec-keys-errors)) and look it up in @sec-troubleshooting.
4. **Try one fix**, the one that line points to, and run the command again.

If that fix does not work, catch up, then open the output the checkpoint's README names and see
that it shows what the book describes.

![Catching up from a checkpoint. Your work is backed up first, so nothing is lost.](media/diagrams/catch-up){#fig-catch-up .on-light fig-alt="Stuck for two minutes, you paste the line Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/NN/README.md into the agent. It follows four steps. One, back up your project folder, all but its .venv environment, to a new time-stamped folder beside it. Two, copy the checkpoint in, and for the water project the data if they are missing. Three, render and check a named output. Four, carry on reading from the catch-up box: the project now matches the book at that point."}

The README ends by naming a workshop slide to rejoin at; in the book, carry on reading from
the catch-up box, even if you were stuck before it, since the checkpoint holds the steps in
between. @sec-checkpoints lists every checkpoint.

## Free and open source, nearly all the way {.unnumbered #open-source}

Almost everything this book uses is free and open-source software, which you may use, read,
change and share at no cost: Ubuntu, the shell, Git, Python and its packages, uv, Jupyter, and
the publishing chain itself, Quarto, Pandoc and Typst (@sec-facts has their licences). That
matters for more than price. A report built from open tools can be rebuilt by anyone, anywhere,
years from now, without a licence, an account or a vendor's permission, and its source is plain
text you own. The exception is the coding agent: its program may be open source, but the
models that do its reasoning are mostly proprietary, run on the vendors' servers and usually
cost money. It is also the one part you could swap without touching a single source file.

## Two editions {.unnumbered #two-editions}

This book comes as an e-book (EPUB) and as a website, built from the same source: it is its
own first example of the method. The [website edition](https://project-delphi.github.io/quarto-workshop/book/)
runs everything interactive: the 3-D scenes of the London map, the k-means steps, the
clusters and Colombia's relief, and two data explorers. The e-book shows each as an animation
or a still, with a link to the live version (the first, the London map, also has a QR code).
Readers that cannot play animations show the first frame, designed as a useful still, and the
website respects your reduced-motion setting.

## Versions and dates {.unnumbered}

The book was built and checked with Quarto 1.10.20 (with its bundled Typst 0.15), Python 3.12
and uv, in November 2026. Facts that change, such as a model's price, an agent's account
or a free hosting plan's limits, carry the date they were checked, and are kept in one place,
@sec-facts, which a rebuild updates everywhere they appear. Some will have changed by the
time you read them; the principles around them
should not have.

@sec-quarto needs nothing installed: start there.
